While I understand that the right wing option is always going to be less regulation on companies, sometimes regulations are needed. The basic function of a (good) government is to make sure that society overall works best for the majority of it's citizens. Since the corps that provide the service in question were moving to a model on a service that would price gouge society as a whole, and the majority of citizens absolutely rely on that service as a basic part of life, stepping in to regulate was the correct choice. The issue overall has become unnecessarily politicized though, so you'll see disagreements of opinion. It happens. Sucks, but it happens.

Usually, you can't go wrong by saying that the feds can't touch something. The net neutrality debate is actually twisted. It's framed as either: 1) regulating ISP and other larger entities to prevent them from creating unfair traffic rules or otherwise abusing their position. OR 2) Leave the industry alone and let free market competition resolve anti-consumer practices. Of course, companies like Comcast would never have gotten where they are without basically having the government work for them, so it's funny that the government says it will come in after the fact and clean things up. If all was right in the world, states would probably be left with the power to ensure competition exists in local markets. This would mean that when things like municipal ISPs rise up, Comcast can't try to block them in the court system.

On a final note, Netflix has a lot of controversy around it that has been misconstrued in various ways. They are large enough to set up peering agreements with various ISPs. They have been accused of having fast lanes into or within ISPs, but peering is not really the same as a fast lane. Pure peering would just be an agreement to exchange traffic as defined points with defined rules. However, the real problem is that shady things go on in peering agreements, but more the point, there is also shady traffic shaping going on within the ISP itself. This is why Netflix tries to make it easy for ISPs to choose not to fuck with their traffic; if there is a peering agreement that means traffic will leave an ISP's network sooner, there is not really a good reason to traffic shape. In essence, only the ISPs should be accused of creating fast lanes for profit, but they actually need to stop all kinds of fuckery. They need to understand that their primary job is to pass traffic to the Internet at large. If they can't do that effectively for all their customers, they need to build a larger or faster network.

I think you are familiar with this at a higher level than I am, but I think I got it. Makes sense. If you are talking about letting the FTC create rules, i.e. regulating the internet possibly as a common carrier, then I wouldn't call it an even playing field. I also don't know what agreements would still be possible, but there may be plenty of ways to work around a regulatory framework as well as exploit the government in ways that are probably reminiscent of Enron. The way I see it, you can only support regulation on the grounds that ISPs are getting away with anti-consumer practices already. However, regulation will only try to make ISPs less bad. They won't deal with any of the problems we are seeing in an intelligent way. They will essentially allow ISPs to become regulated monopolies in many markets. This may keep them operating at an "acceptable" level according to some government standard and make them, for the most part, affordable to consumers, but there will still be many problems in this system, the least of which is the inherent complacency.

There are many reasons why you classifying the Internet as a common carrier isn't suitable: https://www.ncta.com/platform/public-policy/why-its-a-good-thing-that-broadband-isnt-a-common-carrier/ One of those reasons is that there aren't many sources of innovation in this kind of system. The government's interference acts as slow, small bottleneck on what kind of innovation it will allow or support. For example, you have solar energy credits coming from the government, which may make you think great, the government is driving innovation, but it's not really that simple or clean. The industry that runs the Internet is not comparable to energy industry, and, with the pace of the Internet, by the time the government knows it should allow or support a new innovation, it's already too late.
